questions.text: The module's scorer reads the frozen model's next-token scores and picks the label whose first token scores highest. Why not sample a reply and parse it?
options: Sampling would be too slow on a laptop
So the same instruction always gets the same score: a change in score is then a change in the instruction, not luck
Because Qwen3 cannot write the label words
Because DSPy requires it
questions.explain: A search compares many candidates by their scores. If the score had sampling noise in it, the best-looking candidate would often just be the luckiest. Reading next-token scores is greedy and deterministic, so only the instruction moves the number.

questions.text: Each run may score 2,400 training questions. A GEPA-style child costs 6 to test on its minibatch, plus 60 more if it wins. If every child won, how many children could one run test after the baseline's own full pass?
questions.explain: 2,400 − 60 = 2,340 left; each winning child costs 66; 2,340 / 66 = 35.4, so 35. In the real runs only 43% of children won, which is why each run could try about 74.

questions.text: Over 3 seeds the TextGrad-style loop took 117 edit steps. How many raised training accuracy?
questions.explain: 12 raised it, 4 left it equal, and 101 lowered it and were undone. A gradient step with a small enough learning rate lowers the loss on its own batch every time; a critique applied as an edit has no size and no guaranteed sign.

questions.text: Candidate A is right on questions 1–4 of 6, B on 1 and 5, C on 2 and 3. Which are on the Pareto front that GEPA-style search draws parents from?
options: A only: it has the best average
A and B
A, B and C
B and C
questions.explain: A is best on questions 1–4 and B is the only one right on question 5, so both are best somewhere and neither dominates the other. C is right only where A is also right, so A dominates C. Parents are drawn with weight equal to the questions each is best on: A 4, B 2.

questions.text: The baseline scores 60.0% on train and 55.3% on held-out; the chosen instructions lose 8.4 to 10.1 points from train to held-out. What is the best reading?
options: The held-out set is harder than train, so every instruction loses the same
The optimisers saw the held-out questions
The chosen instructions lose about 4 to 5 points more than the baseline's own gap: the cost of picking the best of many candidates on 60 questions
The gap shows the model's weights changed
questions.explain: The baseline's 4.7-point gap is chance: 60 questions are few. Beyond it, the winners lose another 3.8 to 5.4 points. With a standard error near 5.6 points on 60 questions, the best of 30 to 40 candidates tends to have been lucky: the winner's curse.

questions.text: TextGrad-style seed 2 scores 69.7% on held-out but 51.6% on TREC's test set. What explains most of the drop?
options: It saw the test questions
Test questions are longer than the context allows
Float32 scoring changed its answers
Test has a different label mix (28% description, 23% number), and this instruction gets 9% of descriptions and 34% of numbers right
questions.explain: Train and held-out have 10 and 50 questions per label; test follows its own mix. An instruction that rarely says "description" and misses many numbers loses most where test has most. Its gain over the baseline on test is not significant (sign test, p = 0.36).

questions.text: Which of these did the module find in the chosen instructions? Pick all that apply.
options: TextGrad-style winners quote 1 or 2 training questions each
Some instructions quote held-out questions
The TextGrad-style and GEPA-style winners are longer than APE's on average
OPRO's best instruction turned up in the last 15% of its budget in every seed
questions.explain: TextGrad-style winners share a five-word run with 1 or 2 training questions and none with held-out or test. They average 165 words and GEPA-style 147, against APE's 61. OPRO found its best after 240 to 360 of its 2,400 questions; the rest found nothing better.

questions.text: The hand-written instruction against the baseline on 500 test questions: it is right where the baseline is wrong on 77, and wrong where it is right on 42. Why does the sign test ignore the other 381?
options: Where both are right or both are wrong, the questions say nothing about which instruction is better
They were scored with a different model
They are held-out questions
The test only allows 119 questions
questions.explain: Only disagreements carry information. If the two instructions were equally good, each disagreement would be a coin flip; a 77–42 split has p = 0.0017 under that coin.

questions.text: Which hold for the prompt search in this module, and not for gradient descent on weights? Pick all that apply.
options: The parameter has no derivative: accuracy is a step function of a string
There is a held-out set that measures overfitting
A step can store a training example verbatim in the parameter
What makes the score climb is a rule that keeps or drops each proposal
questions.explain: Held-out sets are common to both. The others are particular to text: no smooth neighbourhood, no step size; quoting a training question outright; and a sampler whose draws are kept or dropped, which makes it a search, closer to module 35's evolution than to module 14's optimisers.

questions.text: Why does the module score DSPy's found instruction with its own scorer, besides reporting DSPy's own accuracy?
options: DSPy cannot compute accuracy
Our scorer is faster than DSPy
DSPy wraps the instruction in its own prompt format and parses generated text, so its number is not comparable with our runs; our fixed template and scorer are
DSPy's instruction is in another language
questions.explain: Same instruction, different frame, different number. Putting DSPy's instruction into our fixed template and scorer is the only way to compare it with the twelve hand-built runs on the same footing.
